SEC-HD-V8-01.note: Head noun 'shipment' is singular; 'since the war' forces present perfect. The only item in the whole agreement family whose key is a perfect form, and it is licensed by an explicit 'since' - see cross-item note.

SEC-HD-V8-02.note: Appositive opened with a comma must close with a comma, not a dash; subject 'The east range' is singular. DEFECT: the predicate nominative 'the only stretch' sits three words after the blank and settles number on its own, so a solver who never locates the subject still gets 'remains'. Only the comma/dash half then remains, and that is decidable from the opening comma alone.

SEC-HD-V8-03.note: 'who' is the subject of 'had falsified' ('whom' here is the classic hypercorrection), and the clause is restrictive because it identifies which of four partners. But (D) - same correct case, nonrestrictive commas - is fully well-formed edited English; it is excluded ONLY by the discourse fact that identification is needed, not by any rule. That is a meaning judgement, not a conventions judgement, and a well-prepared student can defend D.

SEC-HD-V8-04.note: Dangling-participle item: the one who lost the count must be a person, so 'the observer'; 'and the expedition came home' fixes simple past over present perfect. Clean two-axis item.

SEC-HD-V8-05.note: 'not only' before the blank demands 'but also', and the parallel term must be a noun phrase matching 'the number of stoppages'. Easy for the hard route: (B) dies on the correlative, (C)/(D) on the repeated verb, all without reading the passage properly.

SEC-HD-V8-06.note: 'more than one of the twelve tenants' takes a singular verb by the standard rule, and 'In the season the estuary silted' forces simple past. (C) 'were turned away' is defensible: MWDEU records plural agreement with 'more than one of' + plural noun (partitive attraction), and many editors accept it. If the key is B this is the item most likely to draw a legitimate protest.

SEC-HD-V8-07.note: TWO DEFECTS. (1) Shape tell: no comma ever precedes a restrictive 'that', so (C) and (D) are eliminable with the passage covered - half the option set gone for free. (2) The stem appears to be a FRAGMENT under every option: 'The surveyors' notebooks that still survive in the same archive, and they record...' has no main verb in its first clause. If the 'that' is intended, the sentence is ungrammatical whatever you pick; if it is a typo for no relativiser, the item is fine. Someone should read the source stem.

SEC-HD-V8-08.note: Sense verb 'smell' takes a predicate adjective, not an adverb; subject 'A cellar' is singular. Two independent axes, both decidable, no ambiguity.

SEC-HD-V8-09.note: 'each of the four pits' is singular and the resurveying is anterior to the 1861 request, so past perfect passive. (D) 'was already resurveyed' is the nearest miss - acceptable in informal AmE where the simple past absorbs the anterior, but not in edited AmE with an explicit 'when ... finally asked in 1861' frame. Marginal call; I would not ship this one without a second opinion.

SEC-HD-V8-10.note: Gerund-phrase subject 'reconciling the entries...' is singular; 'In the years the wharf was in use' closes the period, so simple past. Same two-axis mould as 06/11/18/20.

SEC-HD-V8-11.note: 'as well as' does not compound the subject, so singular; 'when the bandmaster retired' / 'spent forty years' forces simple past. Near-duplicate of 12 and 14 in construction (additive phrase between subject and verb).

SEC-HD-V8-12.note: 'along with' does not compound; subject 'The tracings' is plural, and the sense is passive, so 'were lost'. Easy because both active-progressive options are semantically impossible ('the tracings were losing') without any passage work.

SEC-HD-V8-13.note: Three-item infinitive series: 'to sample..., to weight..., and to record...'. Decidable from the two visible 'to'-phrases before the blank alone.

SEC-HD-V8-14.note: GENUINELY AMBIGUOUS. I read the possessive as agreeing with the plural grammatical subject 'The two presses', giving 'their remaining type was' (tense parallel to 'were sold'). But (C) 'its remaining type was' has an equally available antecedent in 'the font of Cyrillic' - type IS what a font is made of, so 'its remaining type' is arguably the BETTER reading, and nothing in the sentence rules it out. A pronoun-agreement item whose antecedent is contestable is defective as a conventions item; recommend rewrite or kill.

SEC-HD-V8-15.note: Best item in the batch. 'contains,' opens an interrupter that must close before the direct object: 'contains, in the same wallet as the awards themselves, a list of every hedge'. (C) and (D) each insert a comma between 'a list' and its 'of'-complement. Partial help from after the blank ('of every hedge' kills the trailing comma) but the A/B decision still needs the opening comma sixteen words earlier.

SEC-HD-V8-16.note: Appositive 'a volume rebound so often...' must be closed with a comma before the main verb 'records'. (A)'s colon would need a complete clause before it and gets one only if the appositive is left unclosed. Same underlying mould as 02 and 22 (close the interrupter).

SEC-HD-V8-17.note: BROKEN - THREE defensible options. Only (A) is an outright error (comma splice). (B) 'convenience. Consequently the series...' is correct: the comma after an initial conjunctive adverb is optional in Chicago and AP. (C) 'convenience; consequently the series...' is correct for the same reason. (D) is correct and merely fullest-pointed. I picked D only because it is the maximally punctuated option, which is a guess about the author's taste, not about English. Recommend kill or rewrite so that exactly one boundary mark is legal.

SEC-HD-V8-18.note: 'not only X but also Y' takes proximity agreement with 'the village schoolmaster', so singular; 'In the decade after the first policies were sold' forces simple past. Shares the correlative machinery with 05 and the agreement/tense grid with 06/10/11/20.

SEC-HD-V8-19.note: 'The remains ... are' - plural head, and the surrounding present tense ('a dozen days a year', 'what is left') fixes present. Clean.

SEC-HD-V8-20.note: Head noun 'The clauses' is plural across a long relative modifier; the sixty-year window is closed, so simple past. Structurally the same item as 01 with the number and the tense both flipped.

SEC-HD-V8-21.note: Third conditional: 'would have collapsed' in the main clause forces 'had reached' in the if-clause. Easy even on the hard route - 'If ... would have' is a memorised pair and (A) is the standard 'would have in the if-clause' trap.

SEC-HD-V8-22.note: Introductory subordinate clause takes a comma; the following relative clause is restrictive and takes none. Note the option set is unusually transparent in SHAPE: exactly one option has a single leading comma and no internal commas, which is the answer profile for 'comma before, none after'.

SEC-HD-V8-23.note: Backshift in reported speech after 'reported in 1889' kills both 'will' options; 'exhaust' is not used intransitively of a seam, killing (B). Two of the three distractors go on shape/verb-frame grounds alone.

SEC-HD-V8-24.note: 'one of the very few works ... that credit' - the relative attaches to the plural 'works'. Restrictive 'that' takes no comma, so (C) and (D) are eliminable on shape alone with the passage covered, exactly as in 07. (B) 'that credits' is the intended trap; the singular is common in speech but the plural is required in edited English, so I did not flag it as second-defensible - though it is the closest call in the batch after 09.

cross_item_heuristic.guessable_across_items: PARTIALLY YES - one heuristic fired repeatedly and I used it.
cross_item_heuristic.heuristic: Reject any option built on 'have been' / 'has been' / 'have gone' / 'has gone' unless the sentence contains an explicit duration marker ('since', 'for'). The agreement family in this batch (01, 06, 09, 10, 11, 12, 14, 18, 19, 20) presents the same 2x2 grid every time - singular/plural crossed with simple/perfect - and every one of those passages is anchored to a closed past period ('In the season the estuary silted', 'when the bandmaster retired', 'that night', 'In the decade after'). The perfect options are therefore dead on arrival in 9 of the 10, which collapses a four-way choice into a two-way agreement decision before any close reading. The single exception is 01, which carries 'since the war' and IS the perfect. So the rule 'perfect iff since/for is present' fired on 10 of 10 and was never wrong.
cross_item_heuristic.fire_rate: 10 of the 10 agreement/tense items; ~42% of the batch. It does not by itself produce the key (the agreement axis still has to be solved), but it halves every one of those option sets without the passage.
cross_item_heuristic.second_heuristic: Comma before 'that': in 07 and 24 the two comma-bearing options are eliminable on shape alone, since restrictive 'that' never takes a preceding comma. Fired 2 of 2. Same free half-elimination.
cross_item_heuristic.third_heuristic_that_did_NOT_hold: 'The key is the longest / most punctuated option' - I leaned on it only in 17 and have no confidence in it. Across the batch the key is short about as often as long.
cross_item_heuristic.key_letter_distribution_of_my_picks: A:6 (02,05,07,14,19,24)  B:6 (03,04,06,15,16,20)  C:6 (08,09,11,13,22,23)  D:6 (01,10,12,17,18,21). If the real key is also 6/6/6/6, note that a perfectly flat cohort histogram is precisely what hid the 'complete ABCD permutation per group' tell recorded in CLAUDE.md - check the per-group sequence, not just the totals. My picks also never repeat a letter more than twice in a row and cycle A-B-C-D within several consecutive spans (08-13 reads C,C,D,C,D,C; 19-24 reads A,B,D,C,C,A), which is worth a per-window check.
cross_item_heuristic.honesty: Items 03, 06, 14 and 17 are guesses about the author's intent rather than confident readings of English. 09 and 24 are confident but contested.

template_groups.note: Nine of 24 items - 37.5% - are the same agreement-plus-tense grid with a different noun phrase. On a real module-2 hard route SEC is roughly a third of the section but is spread across punctuation, agreement, tense, pronouns and parallelism; this batch is heavily overweight one mould. 01 and 20 are the same item with number and tense both inverted, and 11/12 differ only in the additive phrase used. Recommend thinning that family before insert.
